name: Bilal Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and this conversation is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior buyer at a car parts distributor. We supply about four hundred independent garages with brake pads, filters, wiper blades, batteries, that kind of thing, and garages expect parts within two hours. I look after filters and batteries, so I'm watching stock levels, placing orders with six main suppliers and sorting out what's late. I've been there just over a year and I'm still learning which part numbers cross over between brands.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best is when a garage rings in a panic and I find the last battery in the region at another depot. Worst is the part number tables, there are thousands, and I still get them wrong sometimes. My team leader, Hassan, says it took him three years to stop making those mistakes, which makes me feel a bit better.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Sanne, she's a nurse on a surgical ward. We rent a small terraced house and we've got about four months of costs saved between us. Her job's about as safe as they come, which helps me sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a useful tool and that's it. I use it now and then to write a polite chaser email to a supplier who's late. I wouldn't really post about it either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine. The part-number lookup might get a bit quicker, which would honestly help me. Sanne's job is steady, we've got four months saved, and garages always need parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and focus on learning the cross-reference tables properly. If the company brings in an AI lookup tool and Hassan likes it, I'd use it. Otherwise nothing changes, we'd keep saving for a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That one feels like normal life, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your work that worries you, even with AI at this level?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Electric cars worry me more than AI. Electric cars don't need oil filters, and filters are half my range. That's a slow change, though, over ten years, and batteries and brakes still sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the deposit you're saving for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A two-bed near the hospital, so Sanne can walk to work. We need about fifteen thousand more. At our pace that's three years, if nothing goes wrong.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool** and that's it, without posting either way.
I'd mention using it now and then for **chaser emails** to late suppliers.
think: A quicker **part-number lookup** would honestly help me as a junior.
With Sanne's **steady job** and four months saved, we'd be fine.
do: Learn the **cross-reference tables** for filters and batteries properly.
Use an **AI lookup tool** if the company brings one in and Hassan likes it.
Keep saving towards the **fifteen thousand** still needed for a deposit.
feel: **Calm**, because this picture feels like normal life.
S0.quote: Electric cars worry me more than AI. Electric cars don't need oil filters, and filters are half my range.
fieldNote: His real long-term worry is **electric cars**, not AI.
Sanne's **nursing job** and four months saved anchor his sense of security.
He'd adopt tools once his **team leader** approves them, fitting his steady style.

steps.text: Learn the filter and battery cross-reference tables properly
Use the AI part lookup once Hassan has tried it
Save the fifteen thousand still needed for a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people need to be sensible about it, not panic and not pretend. I'd tell my mates in other jobs to start looking at what their firms are buying. At work I'd say let's see what the system can actually do before anyone gets scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the buying team halves. A system that knows every garage's history can order filters better than me, especially since I still get part numbers wrong. Hassan would stay, he knows the suppliers, and I might not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once Hassan and a couple of others had used the new ordering system for a few months, I'd ask to be trained properly on it. At the same time I'd look at a part-time course to become a vehicle technician, maybe the electric vehicle one at the college. We'd slow down on the deposit and keep more in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd sound fine to Sanne but I'd be checking job sites at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the vehicle technician course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle ran a garage when I was a teenager, and I spent summers handing him spanners. Fixing an electric car is hands-on, so robots get there later. And it's where the trade is heading anyway, with the filters going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sound fine to Sanne. Would you tell her the truth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eventually, yes, she'd see it on my face anyway. Nurses notice everything. I'd just want to have a plan before I told her, so it's not only bad news.

say: I'd say people should be **sensible**, neither panicking nor pretending.
I'd tell colleagues to see what the **system** can do before getting scared.
think: The **buying team halves**, since a system can order filters better than me.
Hassan stays because he **knows the suppliers**, and I might not.
do: Ask for proper **training on the system** once colleagues have used it a few months.
Start a part-time **electric vehicle technician** course at the college.
**Slow down** on the deposit and keep more in the bank.
feel: **Anxious**, sounding fine at home but checking **job sites** at night.
S1.quote: A system that knows every garage's history can order filters better than me, especially since I still get part numbers wrong.
fieldNote: He expects the **team to halve** and sees himself as likely to go.
Summers in his uncle's garage make **EV technician** a believable switch.
He hides worry until he has **a plan**, a quiet pattern in how he copes.

steps.text: Get trained on the new ordering system after colleagues test it
Enrol in the college's part-time electric vehicle technician course
Pause deposit plans and hold more cash in the bank

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and the government needs to sort out support quickly. I'd say it calmly, though, because shouting doesn't help anyone. Online I'd probably just share practical stuff, like where training places are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think I lose my buying job by 2028, no question, it's all desk work. Fixing cars lasts until about 2031 when the robots catch up, so that's my three years. Sanne's job is hands-on and caring, so she's probably the last of us to be touched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the vehicle technician course straight away, full-time if I could get funding, part-time if not. We'd shelve the house completely and keep the deposit money as our cushion. I'd ask my uncle if he knows anyone needing a trainee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Two years is nothing when you're still learning your first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the deposit money in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It stops being a house and becomes eighteen months of my half of the rent. That's hard, because we've been saving it since we moved in. But I'd rather have a roof than a dream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hassan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thanks, honestly, because he taught me a lot. Then I'd say you should think about what you're doing too, because you're at a desk as much as me. He's got two kids, so it's worse for him.

say: I'd say we're **not ready** and the government must sort out support quickly.
I'd share **practical information** like where training places are.
think: My buying job is all **desk work**, so it goes by **2028**.
Car repair lasts until about **2031**, and Sanne's caring work lasts longest.
do: Start the **vehicle technician course** at once, full-time if funded.
**Shelve the house** and keep the deposit as our cushion.
Ask my uncle about **trainee places** at garages he knows.
feel: **Alarmed**, because two years is nothing when still learning a first job.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing when you're still learning your first job.
fieldNote: He separates **desk** from **hands-on** dates clearly and plans around the gap.
The house deposit becomes **eighteen months of rent**, a real loss to him.
He worries for Hassan (his team leader), a desk worker with **two kids**.

steps.text: Start the vehicle technician course this year, funded if possible
Shelve the house purchase with Sanne
Keep the deposit money as an eighteen-month rent cushion
Ask his uncle about trainee places at local garages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning and people should use it. I'd say the same to friends: don't wait for the letter. At work I'd be the one suggesting we all get trained on what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I've got about four years as a buyer, which is enough to qualify as a technician part-time. It lands around 2031, and the robots for garage work come around 2034. So that's maybe seven years of work across both jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep buying, start the part-time technician course next September, and do Saturdays at a garage for experience. We'd still save, but maybe buy a smaller flat instead of a house. I'd use the AI tools at work once they're in, so I understand them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could breathe. It feels like a plan instead of a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A smaller flat instead of a house. Why buy at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sanne wants somewhere that's ours before we have kids. A mortgage on a small flat is about the same as our rent now. If I'm earning less while I train, at least it's not more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said electric cars worry you. Does that fit here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Actually it helps. By 2031 most cars in the garage will be electric, so the training is in the right thing. Funny, the thing I was worried about becomes the thing that saves me.

say: I'd say **five years** is fair warning: **don't wait** for the letter.
At work I'd suggest everyone gets **trained** on what's coming.
think: About **four years** as a buyer is enough to qualify as a technician part-time.
Garage robots come around **2034**, so I'd have about **seven years** of work.
do: Keep buying and start the **technician course** next September.
Work **Saturdays at a garage** for hands-on experience.
Buy a **smaller flat** instead of a house, with a mortgage near current rent.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to breathe because it feels like **a plan**.
S3.quote: By 2031 most cars in the garage will be electric, so the training is in the right thing.
fieldNote: The **five-year gap** lets him stack two jobs end to end.
His earlier worry about **electric cars** turns into his plan.
He still expects his **buying income** to end, so the mood stays anxious.

steps.text: Start the part-time technician course next September
Work Saturdays at a local garage for experience
Use the new AI ordering tools once they arrive
Buy a small flat instead of a house with Sanne

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, as long as people actually start. I'd be quite measured about it. Most people at work would probably ignore it until year eight, and I'd say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel pretty okay. I could become a decent buyer, then switch to electric vehicle work around thirty-two. The robots in 2039 are a long way off, and Sanne's job will be steady for ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in buying for three or four years and get good, maybe move up to Hassan's level. Then I'd train for vehicle work while still earning. We'd go ahead with the house, carefully, with a fixed rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly in the background. It's on my mind but it doesn't keep me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, actually. My dad is a bookkeeper, fifty-five, all screen work. My dad would be sixty-five by 2036, so maybe he scrapes through to retirement, maybe not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to him about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try. He'd say don't be daft, numbers need people. But I'd at least ask him to check his pension, because if he goes at sixty-two instead of sixty-seven, that's a different life.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty, as long as people **actually start**.
I'd warn that most colleagues would ignore it until **year eight**.
think: I can become a good buyer, then switch to **electric vehicle work** around thirty-two.
**2039 robots** are far off, and Sanne's job stays steady.
do: Stay in buying three or four years and aim for **Hassan's level**.
Train for **vehicle work** while still earning.
Buy the house carefully with a **fixed-rate** mortgage.
feel: **Uneasy** in the background, on his mind but not keeping him up.
S4.quote: My dad is a bookkeeper, fifty-five, all screen work. My dad would be sixty-five by 2036, so maybe he scrapes through to retirement, maybe not.
fieldNote: With a decade, his own plan feels **comfortable**.
His worry shifts to his dad, a **bookkeeper** nearing retirement.
He'd go ahead with the house, showing **confidence** in the timeline.

steps.text: Stay in buying and work up toward team leader level
Train for electric vehicle work in his early thirties
Buy the house on a fixed-rate mortgage
Ask his dad to check his pension and retirement date

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is too short to retrain when you're junior and still making mistakes. What would help is funding for full-time trade courses for people already working, so you're not choosing between rent and learning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the garages. If the small garages close or get bought up by big chains, it doesn't matter what I'm trained in. The small garages are the customers for everything I do, now and later.

headlineQuote: If the small garages close or get bought up by big chains, it doesn't matter what I'm trained in.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old junior buyer** of filters and batteries at a car parts distributor.
He lives with Sanne, a **nurse**, whose steady job anchors his sense of safety.
He's **steady**: he'd learn new tools once Hassan, his team leader, has tested them.
From Steady Disruption on, he plans to retrain as an **electric vehicle technician**, drawing on summers at his uncle's garage.
His mood rises from **calm** to **alarmed** as the warning shrinks, easing to uneasy with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to retrain as a junior.
whatWouldHelp: Funding for **full-time trade courses** for people already working.
